items.title: [Kagi Small Web] @plotbunnyfarm replied to your post “If it’s any help to anyone, here’s how the…”:
items.content_html:
@plotbunnyfarm replied to your post “If it’s any help to anyone, here’s how the…”:

you have 6 (presumably working) sewing machines, do you use them all? are they set up for different tasks or are they just for the joy of different machines? (said with some admiration, this sounds like a lot of work and knowledge to restore these)

Most of the machine heads are working, but a lot of them still need work of some kind! When more of them are in a usable condition I definitely will use multiple of them, since they’re pretty diverse and have different advantages.

This 30’s or 40’s Singer 15-91 is the first machine I bought, because I needed a sewing machine when I moved out. It’s been my main machine for the past 7 years, and I hadn’t gotten into refurbishing machines then, so this is the only one I bought already refurbished.

This is an old picture, I recently refinished the case and haven’t gotten photos yet!
It’s a good straight stitch machine and I like it. I suppose the motor could probably benefit from being opened up and cleaned, but it’s controlling better than it was before I bought a new pedal a couple years ago.

This is a “Gimbels” branded Japanese clone of a Singer 15, which I bought at a garage sale because it was $20 and sad and needed my help. I cleaned it all up and it works, but the wooden case was too rotten to save, so I need to get some help to build a new one.
It’s very similar to the 15-91, but there are some differences! It’s got a more obvious drop feed than the hidden one on the 15-91, and a slightly lower feed setting for delicate fabrics. There are little spring loaded plugs on all the top oil holes to keep dust out, and a few other minor differences.
Once I get a new case built for it I’ll sew on it and see how I feel about it. I may re-home one of these machines someday, or maybe even both, depending on which machines I end up using most in future. It’s cool that these can share bobbins, but functionally they’re so similar that I don’t need to keep both forever, especially if I end up having a favourite.

I could pop it in the 15-91 case and give it a go now, actually. Maybe I will do that.

The 99k I recently gave to a friend came from the same garage sale, but I was able to fix the case because it was less damaged. Probably stored on a higher shelf in the same damp room.

The reason I chose the Singer 99k to give away was because I have a Singer 185J, which is a later version of the same model!

Like the Gimbels, it works but I have not used it because the case was a wreck and I need to build a new one. (Since it fits in a 99 case I measured that one before gifting it.)

This does have a different advantage. It’s a ¾ size “portable” model, so everything is a bit smaller, including the feed dogs. And WOW do the shorter feed dogs ever make a difference in turning curves! I was amazed by how tightly I could turn without pivoting when I tried out the finished 99k!
Since I love making leaf themed clothing with serrated edges, I will take advantage of this on future leaf projects.

I took some photos of them together before putting the 99k back in its case, to show how the 185J is really just a 99k in green space age pyjamas. I have so many other black machines and am a sucker for that shade of green, so I kept that one.

The 1885 White VS2 works, but the needle size is a bit troublesome. I have a few precious original needles, which are very long, and the closest modern ones I found are round shank and I can’t get them tightened securely enough in the needle clamp.

They would be fine if I could just file a little dent into the needle shanks, but none of my metal files are hard enough. I could lower the needle bar and use industrial needles, but I have so many other machines that I know my main one will never be one that can’t backstitch, so I can just be gentle with the original needles and maybe eventually get flat bits filed on the modern ones.

I would like to use this for patchwork, since that’s something I don’t need to backstitch for. I haven’t done a patchwork project in a while, but I have plans for some.
Even if I don’t use it very often, it’s nice to have in my bedroom, and it came with a lot of provenance. I know who owned it and made her living sewing on it from approximately the 1910’s until 1984, and I’ve looked at some of her diaries in person. (We’re not related, her much younger cousin is a friend of my uncle’s and he gave me the machine. No clue who owned it for the first few decades of its existence.)

Ooooh hot damn! The 1945 Bernina treadle!!! It’s a KL 105, the first model Bernina ever made for the home sewing market, and apparently a very rare find here in Canada.

This was given to me earlier this year and I am SO excited to get to use it. I’ve got the machine head all clean and it’s stitching fine and I have needles that fit, and I’m currently in the process of refurbishing the treadle table. It needs a lot of work but I hope to get it done soon, while the weather is still good for working outdoors.

It’s a rotary treadle with backstitch AND drop feed! What a dream! It’ll be so smooth and quiet!! It’s got markings in METRIC! It also has a darning/embroidery foot, and it came with a specialized darning hoop for socks. It has so much drawer space.

Look at this stitch length adjustor.

I’m keeping this one forever and ever. It’s too early to say, since I haven’t been able to properly use it yet and I have very little experience with treadles, but there’s a distinct possibility that this could become my new main machine.

Ah, the Pfugly Pfaff 360 from 1970. This was my second ever machine, and I bought it for $25 at an estate sale just because I was having trouble with my 15-91 speed control and I wanted a backup.
Once I got home I learned that it was a really good machine, and also that the innards were very gummed up with the hardened remains of an anti-rust protective wax the manufacturers sprayed in there. I got most of it loose, but the side to side motion is still stuck.

It sews, but currently only in a tiny shitty zigzag. I borrowed a tool from my father to take it apart and get it unstuck, but I haven’t done that yet. It is on my list of goals for this year.
It just makes me a bit nervous to mess with machines this new, I worry I’ll break one of the plastic knobs or something. I already snapped the light switch off while putting the lid on :(

Once I do unstick that part it’ll be able to do zigzag, and an assortment of fancy stitches with this nifty stack of cams. All my other machines are straight stitch and I’ve never had a zigzag machine, so that’ll be cool!
I can live just fine without zigzag, but it will be very nice to have it.
It’s also my only machine where the bed folds down to give you a smaller round bit to sew around, and it came with a darning foot, so maybe once it’s unstuck I’ll get around to mending some of my worn out pants inseams.

The cute little Western Electric in the previous post is very new to me, but I’m excited to try it once I get it all cleaned up and fitted with a hand crank. This 1911 book on free motion treadle embroidery blew my mind, and I do want to try that stuff on my Bernina treadle, but I also really want to try it on a hand crank because I suspect it’ll be easier to place the needle precisely.

And the industrial serger! c. 1970s, with a later motor. What a ridiculous stroke of luck. What an absolute steal. Everyone is correct to be jealous.
I’ve done the oil change and cleaned out the dust filter, so all this beast needs now is for me to repaint some markings that have worn off. I don’t count this in the sewing machine number, since it’s a different thing.
I shall have nice clean finished edges in all my pants without having to go across town to use Mama’s serger.

So that’s my current herd!
Getting the machine head all cleaned up is the fun part, and I can do it at home, but the woodworking stuff is a lot harder since I haven’t really got the tools or space for most of it. I need to get some wood for those 2 cases, and then will get Papa to help, since he has a table saw.
The Western Electric case and Bernina table are going to be sanded, patched, and refinished outdoors because I have no garage, and I need to hurry up before it gets too cold.

I’ve done so much work on so many machines that it seems really weird to still have so few that are actually 100% usable, but they’re getting there! Someday I will have multiple in rotation for different tasks!

Also, since you mentioned knowledge, I would like to once again say that I fell into this accidentally just a couple years ago and pretty much all I knew when I started was how to oil and sew on one. But I looked lots of stuff up on the internet, and learned by taking stuff apart and photographing as I go, and there’s always more I’m learning! Every newly acquired gunky machine is a new adventure.
